About a third of food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according UN data. Photograph: Rich Pedroncelli/AP Food waste Plastics contamination an ‘overlooked’ concern in food waste schemes, experts say Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils Ushika Kidd Sun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call one of the most overlooked problems of the climate crisis, researchers have said. This is despite the fact that, as the chef, author and activist Max La Manna puts it, food waste management is “one of the few climate problems where everyone wins”. About one-third of all food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according to UN data. In the US, 40% of food waste goes to landfill, where it creates 30m metric tonnes of CO 2 equivalent a year – more than Cuba’s total annual CO 2 emissions in 2024, which amounted to 24.4m tonnes. A new study, published in Nature Food , used life-cycle analysis modelling to compare the impacts – in terms of climate, nutrient pollution and plastic contamination – of different food-waste management scenarios. The authors, based at the University of Vermont, compared the annual climate impacts of landfilled food waste with the climate impact of alternative recycling pathways and found that diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%. These non-landfill scenarios could also reduce nutrient pollution in water bodies – a process called eutrophication that occurs when excess nutrients result in algal blooms. But the researchers also said that microplastics can persist in compost, which could lead to 20,000 tonnes contaminating US agricultural soils each year. To date, no study has looked at the “plastic pollution footprint” of different food-waste management strategies at national scale. Kate Porterfield, the lead author, said the method was comparable to working out a “carbon footprint of a product or process”. Essentially, the researchers looked at the process of managing food waste and “tall[ied] up what the carbon emissions are across all of those life-cycle stages”, she said. Porterfield said the large proportion of wasted food still in packaging “goes bad before it even reaches the consumer”. One approach to recycling food waste is using a mechanical “depacker”; the packaging then goes to landfill, while food waste goes to “beneficial reuse, like composting or anaerobic digestion”. However, they found that even if plastic separation technologies were 99% efficient, diverting food waste from landfill could still increase microplastic pollution in soil by an order of magnitude. “Any time where you’re diverting food waste, there is a risk of microplastic pollution” because “people aren’t perfect, machines aren’t perfect, and all of our food these days is packaged in plastic”. The US state of Vermont has “one of the most ambitious” state organics-diversion mandates in the US, according to the co-author Eric Roy. The state’s Universal Recycling Law has been fully effective from 2020 and requires food waste to be diverted from landfill. This applies to all households and means food scraps are banned from bins. The authors said their findings provided an effective evaluation of the possible countrywide scale-up of such regulations and pointed to the need for “more attention to the plastics issue” from the outset of creating these policies. Phil Holtam, a co-founder and director of the food waste social enterprise Sussex Surplus, said there was “a little bit of a misconception that [plastic packaging] is unnecessary”, and that it was a “necessary tradeoff”, essential to extending the shelf life of fresh produce, particularly for smallholder farms. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Preview latest after newsletter promotion “That’s where the tension lies because as environmentalists we want to reduce food waste but we also want to prevent needless use of plastics.” La Manna, who has worked with farmers in the UK and also witnessed food waste working in a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York, said consumer expectations of perfect-looking food were shaping what produce even made it to store shelves and adding to the waste problem. “Some of it may be misshapen, wonky, slightly cosmetically imperfect … [which is] challenging for supermarkets because they believe consumers want a perfect cucumber. “We’re allowing ‘perfect’ to become this enemy of good.” Roy underlined that in institutions such as schools, there “may be some well-intentioned rules that actually create challenges in moving away from highly packaged foods” because “food safety is always going to be a number one concern”. Porterfield said that, ultimately, to reduce plastic contamination food waste management systems needed to be “as easy as possible to make it mindless for people to separate things efficiently”. This included addressing the phenomenon of “wish recycling”, said Roy, where people put non-recyclable items in recycling in the hope they will be recycled. He advised “old-school environmentalism” to reduce litter overall: “buy in bulk”, “make every effort to separate” – and “if in doubt, put it in the landfill stream”. Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian design Australian immigration and asylum China expresses ‘grave concern’ as internal documents reveal suicide warning before death in Melbourne immigration detention Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Christopher Knaus and Ariel Bogle Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US private prison company running Australia’s immigration system was warned that a newly detained Chinese citizen expressed suicidal ideation and had a history of self-harm less than 24 hours before she died by suicide in a Melbourne detention centre, internal documents show. The death has raised serious questions about whether the detainee was properly monitored and whether she was placed in an appropriate room, given her state of mind. It has also triggered an intervention from Australia’s biggest trading partner, Guardian Australia can reveal. Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention network Read more The Chinese embassy has confirmed it has “lodged solemn representations and expressed grave concern to the Australian side” about the circumstances of the death. “China will closely follow the case and safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens,” an embassy spokesperson said. China’s public intervention creates a fresh headache for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke , who is already furious about a string of security lapses involving the government’s new immigration contractor, Secure Journeys, a local subsidiary of the US-based prison multinational Management and Training Corporation. In May the Guardian revealed that a series of failures had allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised and triggered multiple investigations, one of which warned that MTC’s “minimalist staffing model” was putting workers and detainees at risk. Burke took the extraordinary step of hauling in the global president of MTC for a face-to-face dressing down in September 2025, just six months after the company was awarded the $2.3bn onshore immigration detention contract. On 10 July Australian Border Force issued a short statement saying a detainee had been found dead in the Melbourne immigration detention centre that morning. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The detainee was a Chinese citizen in her mid-30s who had been picked up the day before for allegedly overstaying an English-language studies visa, internal documents seen by the Guardian show. She had no criminal history. The ABF transferred her into the custody of Secure Journeys on the afternoon of 9 July. The ABF made clear to Secure Journeys that she had previously attempted self-harm and had “recently thought about self-harm/suicide”, the documents show . She was found hanging in her room in the Broadmeadows residential precinct, part of the Melbourne immigration detention centre, early the next morning. Victoria police are investigating the death, which they described as non-suspicious. The coroner’s court of Victoria said it had directed police to prepare a brief of evidence. Illustration: Guardian Design / Rich Cousins There were 360 reported incidents of threatened and actual self-harm across Australia’s onshore immigration detention network between July 2025 and March 2026, according to parliamentary records. There have been at least two deaths this year. A Secure Journeys spokesperson said the company offered its “deep condolences to the family and friends of the female detainee” but could not comment further due to the investigation. “Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority,” the spokesperson said. The Department of Home Affairs offered sincere condolences to the woman’s family and friends. “Due to our privacy obligations to the deceased and the ongoing investigation into this matter, it would not be appropriate to comment further,” a spokesperson said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion China experts described the embassy’s statement as “firm but not excessive”. The Australia-China Relations Institute’s director, Prof James Laurenceson, said the fact that representations had been made and the embassy had expressed “grave concerns” showed it was taking the death seriously. But Laurenceson said he didn’t read the embassy’s statement as “excessively aggressive”. Labor plans migration cuts as Tony Burke pulls out of major speech Read more “It is the case that Australia and China have been trading tersely worded diplomatic statements more frequently in recent months over everything from Taiwan, China’s maritime claims in the South China Sea, its cyber operations, the Jimmy Lai case, Darwin Port, and more,” he said. “But I am not convinced that China’s statement in this case should be interpreted as some sort of diplomatic slap back for Australian complaints about Chinese actions in other contexts.” MTC’s performance in running Australia’s onshore detention network has triggered multiple investigations, including by the federal work safety regulator Comcare. Internal documents show Comcare has set up a dedicated inspection program to scrutinise immigration detention, citing an “increase in notifiable incidents, the severity and the profile of the reported incidents involving the [contractor]”. The regulator privately warned the department this year that it had received numerous reports of “serious injury or illness to both workers and others (detainees)”, “self-harm ideations and death involving detainees” and “detainee on detainee violence”. One of Comcare’s key concerns is that the risk-assessment system used in the centres is not effective and is putting staff and detainees at serious risk of violence and other harms. Understaffing has been a key concern since MTC took over. A March report by the National Preventive Mechanism, an independent monitor of places of detention, reported that “critically” low staffing levels were compromising the centres’ safety. The understaffing is also causing seriously ill detainees to miss medical appointments because MTC lacks workers to escort them to health centres. * Do you know more? Pakistan: Passenger train derailment kills at least five, injures more than 30 Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 13/10/2026 - 10:04 GMT+2 At least five people were killed and more than 30 injured when the Rehman Baba Express derailed near Multan, Pakistan, early on Tuesday, 13 October. An investigation has been launched into the cause of the accident. … More The Rehman Baba Express , travelling from Karachi to Peshawar, came off the tracks at around 5.15am local time near Sher Shah railway station in Punjab province. All 14 carriages derailed , with several overturning and trapping passengers inside. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Rescue workers, police and local residents searched the wreckage, while cranes were brought in to remove damaged coaches. The injured were taken to Nishtar Hospital in Multan , where at least one person was reported to be in critical condition. Pakistan Railways said all passengers had been evacuated. Train services on the affected line were suspended, and a relief train and medical unit were dispatched to the scene. The cause of the accident remains unknown, and an investigation is under way. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered authorities to accelerate rescue efforts and ensure proper medical care for those injured.
